analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: A Democratic bill creating federal paid family and medical leave was introduced in the House and never received a hearing, vote, or action in committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give workers up to 60 days of paid leave per year to care for a newborn, a seriously ill family member, or their own serious health condition, paying a share of their wages through a new Social Security Administration office. It would be funded by a 0.2 percent payroll tax on both workers and employers (0.4 percent on self-employment income), collected into a new federal trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who need time off for a new child, a serious illness, or to care for an ill or aging family member — especially the vast majority who had no employer-paid leave, only 13% of whom had access per the bill's findings.

how_it_helps.text: Provides monthly wage-replacement benefits (minimum $580, maximum $4,000 initially) for up to 60 caregiving days per benefit period [S3].
Covers leave reasons recognized under the FMLA: own serious health condition, birth/adoption, care of child/spouse/parent, servicemember care and exigencies; includes domestic partners [S3].
Makes it unlawful for employers to fire or discriminate against workers who apply for or receive benefits, with damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers each pay a 0.2 percent payroll tax on wages (0.4 percent total combined); self-employed individuals pay 0.4 percent.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers, via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: New payroll taxes of 0.2% on workers and 0.2% on employers would apply broadly to wages, including employers that already provide paid leave [S3].
Only 60 caregiving days (about 12 weeks) per benefit period, with a five-day waiting period — some workers would need longer coverage than the cap allows [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax burden is small (roughly $150/year for a $75,000 worker) relative to the wage protection provided during leave, but employer compliance and program administration would be significant new federal undertakings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security Subcommittee, where it received no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Referred to Ways and Means, then to the Social Security Subcommittee on 2015-03-19 [S5].
No further actions listed through the end of the 114th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself; workers without paid leave saw no federal program created, while employers avoided the 0.2 percent payroll tax.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 66 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; no hearing or markup was held.

against.name: House Republicans
against.role: Majority controlling the Ways and Means agenda
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee schedule and did not advance the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 137 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill originated with House Democrats and the Ways and Means majority was Republican [S4].

industries.note: Would pay a 0.2% payroll tax, though some employers could coordinate the federal benefit with existing private plans and reduce their own costs [S3].
Some could coordinate their own benefits with the federal program and realize cost savings [S3].
